---
title: "Comparing predictive loss"
---

The [grouped-validation page](grouped-cross-validation.qmd) returned held-out losses to the groups omitted during fitting. Comparing two procedures requires pairing their predictions on those same groups. We now use an ordinal response and hold out complete verb types, which makes both the loss and the new-verb prediction task visible.

## MegaOrientation

[Moon and White (2020)](https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/005282/current.pdf) constructed sentence pairs that force past- or future-oriented interpretations by combining matrix tense or modality with an incompatible embedded temporal adverb. Participants rated the sentences on a 1-to-7 acceptability scale. The corrected [MegaOrientation v1.1 release](https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-orientation/mega-orientation-v1.1.zip) changes the released participant and verb inventories after items with irregular-inflection errors were rerun.

The original paper fits latent lexical, structural, and mixed models with participant-specific ordinal cutpoints. The teaching comparison is narrower. It restricts the release to verbs attested in at least two frames, fits population cumulative-logit models, and holds out every response from a verb together. Thus, the target is an unseen verb within the selected multi-frame inventory, not a reproduction of the paper's latent-type comparison.

The two models are

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_0 &: \text{response}\sim\text{orientation}+\text{frame},\\
M_1 &: \text{response}\sim\text{orientation}*\text{frame}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For response $y_i$, the ordinal log score is

$$
L_i(M)=-\log p_M(Y_i=y_i\mid x_i).
$$

Equivalently, we can compare the log probability itself, where larger values are better. The sign convention below reports $\log p_{M_1}-\log p_{M_0}$, so positive values favor the interaction.

## Held-out-verb comparison

The code loads the tracked response table and frozen verb folds, fits both ordinal models in every fold, and extracts the probability assigned to each observed rating. It first averages log scores within verbs and only then averages the `r length(unique(utils::read.csv("data/megaorientation/verb-folds-multiframe.csv")$verb))` verbs, preventing verbs with more judgment rows from receiving greater weight.

```{r}
#| label: megaorientation-predictive-comparison
#| message: false
#| warning: false

orientation <- utils::read.delim(
  "data/megaorientation/megaorientation-v1.1.tsv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)
verb_folds <- utils::read.csv(
  "data/megaorientation/verb-folds-multiframe.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
orientation <- merge(
  orientation,
  verb_folds[c("verb", "fold")],
  by = "verb",
  sort = FALSE
)
orientation$outcome <- ordered(orientation$response, levels = 1:7)
orientation$orientation <- factor(
  orientation$orientation, levels = c("past", "future")
)
orientation$frame_code <- factor(orientation$frame_code)

stopifnot(all(tapply(
  orientation$fold, orientation$verb,
  function(x) length(unique(x))
) == 1))

ordinal_probabilities <- function(fit, newdata, formula) {
  design <- model.matrix(formula, newdata)
  eta <- drop(design[, names(fit$beta), drop = FALSE] %*% fit$beta)
  cumulative <- plogis(outer(
    eta,
    fit$alpha,
    function(linear_predictor, threshold) {
      threshold - linear_predictor
    }
  ))
  probability <- cbind(
    cumulative[, 1],
    cumulative[, -1, drop = FALSE] -
      cumulative[, -ncol(cumulative), drop = FALSE],
    1 - cumulative[, ncol(cumulative)]
  )
  probability <- pmax(probability, 1e-12)
  probability / rowSums(probability)
}

prediction_rows <- vector("list", length(unique(orientation$fold)))
fold_rows <- vector("list", length(unique(orientation$fold)))

for (fold in sort(unique(orientation$fold))) {
  train <- orientation[orientation$fold != fold, ]
  test <- orientation[orientation$fold == fold, ]

  restricted_fit <- ordinal::clm(
    outcome ~ orientation + frame_code,
    data = train,
    link = "logit",
    Hess = FALSE,
    control = ordinal::clm.control(maxIter = 200L, gradTol = 1e-3)
  )
  interaction_fit <- ordinal::clm(
    outcome ~ orientation * frame_code,
    data = train,
    link = "logit",
    Hess = FALSE,
    control = ordinal::clm.control(maxIter = 200L, gradTol = 1e-3)
  )

  restricted_probability <- ordinal_probabilities(
    restricted_fit, test, ~ orientation + frame_code
  )
  interaction_probability <- ordinal_probabilities(
    interaction_fit, test, ~ orientation * frame_code
  )
  observed <- cbind(seq_len(nrow(test)), as.integer(test$outcome))
  restricted_log_score <- log(restricted_probability[observed])
  interaction_log_score <- log(interaction_probability[observed])

  prediction_rows[[fold]] <- data.frame(
    verb = test$verb,
    fold = fold,
    restricted_log_score = restricted_log_score,
    interaction_log_score = interaction_log_score
  )
  fold_rows[[fold]] <- data.frame(
    fold = fold,
    held_out_verbs = length(unique(test$verb)),
    held_out_rows = nrow(test),
    interaction_minus_restricted = mean(
      interaction_log_score - restricted_log_score
    )
  )
}

predictions <- do.call(rbind, prediction_rows)
fold_scores <- do.call(rbind, fold_rows)
verb_scores <- aggregate(
  predictions[c("restricted_log_score", "interaction_log_score")],
  list(verb = predictions$verb, fold = predictions$fold),
  mean
)
verb_scores$interaction_minus_restricted <- with(
  verb_scores, interaction_log_score - restricted_log_score
)

set.seed(20261106)
verb_bootstrap <- replicate(
  999L,
  mean(sample(
    verb_scores$interaction_minus_restricted,
    nrow(verb_scores),
    replace = TRUE
  ))
)
comparison <- data.frame(
  held_out_rows = nrow(predictions),
  held_out_verbs = nrow(verb_scores),
  row_weighted_gain = mean(
    predictions$interaction_log_score - predictions$restricted_log_score
  ),
  verb_weighted_gain = mean(
    verb_scores$interaction_minus_restricted
  ),
  bootstrap_low = quantile(verb_bootstrap, 0.025, names = FALSE),
  bootstrap_high = quantile(verb_bootstrap, 0.975, names = FALSE),
  folds_favoring_interaction = sum(
    fold_scores$interaction_minus_restricted > 0
  )
)
comparison

ggplot2::ggplot(
  verb_scores,
  ggplot2::aes(factor(fold), interaction_minus_restricted)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0, color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    position = ggplot2::position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0),
    size = 0.8,
      alpha = 0.35, # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    color = "grey25"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = fold_scores,
    ggplot2::aes(factor(fold), interaction_minus_restricted),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2,
    color = "#2B6CB0"
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Held-out verb fold",
    y = "Interaction minus restricted mean log score"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

The interaction improves the verb-weighted mean log score by `r sprintf("%.5f", comparison$verb_weighted_gain)`, with a conditional verb-bootstrap interval of [`r sprintf("%.5f", comparison$bootstrap_low)`, `r sprintf("%.5f", comparison$bootstrap_high)`]. The row-weighted gain is `r sprintf("%.5f", comparison$row_weighted_gain)`, and `r comparison$folds_favoring_interaction` of `r nrow(fold_scores)` folds favor the interaction. The gray points show all held-out verb differences; the blue points show fold means.

## Raw responses and the descriptive fit

The predictive comparison uses held-out verbs. A full-data interaction fit serves a different purpose: it lets us check fitted ordinal probabilities against the empirical rating distribution in each represented frame-orientation cell.

```{r}
#| label: megaorientation-raw-fitted
#| message: false
#| warning: false

full_interaction <- ordinal::clm(
  outcome ~ orientation * frame_code,
  data = orientation,
  link = "logit",
  Hess = FALSE
)
orientation_grid <- expand.grid(
  orientation = levels(orientation$orientation),
  frame_code = levels(orientation$frame_code)
)
orientation_grid$orientation <- factor(
  orientation_grid$orientation,
  levels = levels(orientation$orientation)
)
orientation_grid$frame_code <- factor(
  orientation_grid$frame_code,
  levels = levels(orientation$frame_code)
)
fitted_probability <- ordinal_probabilities(
  full_interaction,
  orientation_grid,
  ~ orientation * frame_code
)

empirical <- as.data.frame(table(
  orientation$frame_code,
  orientation$orientation,
  orientation$outcome,
  dnn = c("frame_code", "orientation", "rating")
))
names(empirical)[4] <- "count"
empirical$empirical_probability <- ave(
  empirical$count,
  empirical$frame_code,
  empirical$orientation,
  FUN = function(x) x / sum(x)
)
fitted <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  seq_len(nrow(orientation_grid)),
  function(index) data.frame(
    frame_code = as.character(orientation_grid$frame_code[index]),
    orientation = as.character(orientation_grid$orientation[index]),
    rating = as.character(seq_len(7)),
    fitted_probability = fitted_probability[index, ]
  )
))
raw_and_fitted <- merge(
  empirical,
  fitted,
  by = c("frame_code", "orientation", "rating"),
  sort = FALSE
)
raw_and_fitted$rating <- as.integer(raw_and_fitted$rating)

ggplot2::ggplot(
  raw_and_fitted,
  ggplot2::aes(rating, empirical_probability, color = orientation)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.4, alpha = 0.75) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    ggplot2::aes(y = fitted_probability),
    linewidth = 0.55
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ frame_code) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(
    values = c("past" = "grey35", "future" = "#2B6CB0") # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_len(7)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Acceptability rating",
    y = "Response probability",
    color = "Forced orientation"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

The tracked comparison contains `r format(nrow(orientation), big.mark = ",")` judgments from `r length(unique(orientation$verb))` multi-frame verbs and `r nrow(unique(orientation[c("verb", "frame_code")]))` predicate-frame pairs. Points are empirical category probabilities; lines are the descriptive full-data interaction fit. Those fitted lines do not supply the held-out comparison numbers.

## Scope of the gain

The conditional bootstrap resamples the stored verb differences while holding the fitted cross-validation predictions fixed. It respects verb as the resampling unit, but it does not reproduce participant, item, or refitting uncertainty. The population models also omit participant and sentence-item effects. Thus, the interval is useful for the paired-loss lesson, not a full confirmatory analysis of the experiment.

The interaction gain suggests that frame-specific orientation patterns help predict ratings for unseen verbs within this selected inventory. It does not turn acceptability into a directly observed temporal-orientation label, reproduce Moon and White's lexical-versus-structural theory comparison, or generalize to unrestricted English embedding verbs.

## Checking the comparison

1. Why does a positive difference favor the interaction model?
2. Why are log scores averaged within verbs before the primary mean is taken?
3. What does the full-data probability plot check, and what does it not estimate?
4. Which omitted sources of dependence limit the bootstrap interval?

A paired comparison evaluates two models on identical held-out groups and returns their differences to the unit specified by the scientific claim. The [previous page](grouped-cross-validation.qmd) developed grouped splitting with Natural Stories. The [next page](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd) begins a five-page Provo sequence using two fixed Gaussian mean models.
